entry.title: Web Engines Hackfest
entry.content:
I will be at [Web Engines Hackfest](https://webengineshackfest.org/, meeting with people who want to figure out where browsers should be going next.

I proposed a breakout on Browser Funding After Search Deals:

Browsers have, for the most part, a simple business model: a search engine pays them in exchange for market share. Over the past two decades, these deals have constrained browser user interfaces into a set of patterns that don't risk interfering with search traffic, have constrained users into continually degrading search experiences, and have organised a system that contributes to defunding the rest of the web.

Thankfully, the legality of these arrangements has been called into question and even though the situation remains fluid, browsers are looking for new sources of revenue. What does that look like? What becomes possible if we are no longer bound by the UX choices of our ancestors in which we have to drive eyeballs to a search engine as fast and often as we can? This session will brainstorm alternatives, will explore both new UX and new business models. Multihoming search? Integrating commerce? Ads? Social? It's all on the table.

If it happens, I hope I'll see you there!

entry.title: Re:publica: How We Can Finally Make The Digital World Democratic
entry.content:
I'm delighted to be speaking at Re:publica, where I'll be giving a talk about "How We Can Finally Make The Digital World Democratic: Starting With Social Media".

The abstract says it all:

Most of the digital sphere is under authoritarian governance: we only get change by begging large companies to act better or sometimes by forcing them. And when you take an authoritarian system and you use it as infrastructure for society, through the power of infrastructure that society becomes authoritarian as well.

We cannot continue this way, but the fact that there is limited experience with democratic governance in the digital sphere makes it challenging to understand how to approach the problem. In this talk, we will see how by using open protocols and technical architectures that are compatible with democracy, and by understanding the role of digital infrastructure, we can build democratic social media.

See you there if you're going!

entry.title: Originator Profile
entry.content:
I had the pleasure of visiting the Originator Profile project in Tokyo. OP is a project bringing together a large group of media companies to develop ways of marking content as authentic.

We discussed various aspects of disinformation and how to label content in ways that respect pluralism and help avoid disinformation at the same time. We also looked at how labelling works on Bluesky, atop the AT Protocol.

Additionally, it was great to get a chance to visit the Yomiuri Shimbun.

entry.title: 'Rewilding' To Feature in 'Best American Science & Nature Writing 2025'
entry.content:
This came as a huge and delightful surprise: We Need To Rewild The Internet, which I co-authored with the mighty Maria Farrell and that was published in April 2024 by Noema has been selected to feature in the classic anthology Best American Science & Nature Writing 2025.

The book will come out later in 2025. I am incredibly excited to hold a physical copy.

entry.title: Digital & Data Sovereignty: Definitions and Technologies for Independence and Resilience
entry.content:
The Graduate Institute hosted an event convened by Emrys Schoemaker to discuss data sovereignty and infrastructure with the wider UN community. The event opened with a keynote from Ambassador Kah, and was followed by a panel moderated by Mark Scott and featuring interventions from Neha Mishra, Konstantinos Komaitis, and yours truly.

We discussed the rising importance of digital sovereignty in global digital governance, and more widely in geopolitics and trade.

This is part of a series of events on digital sovereignty. Several further ones will be announced soon and reports are being prepared.

entry.title: The Next Social Wave: Open, Competitive, and User-Controlled
entry.content:
For years, social media has been dominated by a handful of companies, shaping how information flows, harming our informational enviroment, and limiting innovation. The dangers have never been clearer. But a new paradigm is emerging—one where open protocols, competition, and user choice drive the future of social media.

This panel discussed the Future of Technology Institute (FoTI) whitepaper “Algorithmic Pluralism: Towards Competitive & Innovative Information Ecosystems” which I coauthored with Sherif Elsayed-Ali, bringing us together with Marietje Schaake, former MEP and Stanford University fellow, and Emily Liu, Head of Special Projects at Bluesky.

entry.title: Algorithmic Pluralism: Towards Competitive & Innovative Information Ecosystems
entry.content:
This whitepaper is part of the first in a series on the Open Network Economy (ON Economy), an accelerating shift in the way in which the web works that is characterized by a number of novel behaviors and technologies. We believe this paradigm change is reshaping the economics of the internet — from social media to search, and beyond.

In this instalment, we look at algorithmic pluralism in the information ecosystem. We introduce the concept and its importance across social media, traditional search, and AI search. We then go in more depth on how social media works today and how algorithmic pluralism leads to a more diverse and innovative social web.

You can download “Algorithmic Pluralism: Towards Competitive & Innovative Information Ecosystems” and read it at your convenience!

entry.title: PETs and AI: Privacy Washing and the Need for a PETs Evaluation Framework
entry.content:
Schloss Dagstuhl is a German public institution that hosts research seminars in computer science. I was delighted to be invited to this seminar on PETs and AI: Privacy Washing and the Need for a PETs Evaluation Framework alongside a group of excellent researchers.

The core issue is that PETs (Privacy-Enhancing Technologies) were supposed to undermine power and serve people, but in practice they often focus on confidentiality and not privacy, serve to legitimate inappropriate processes, and their deployment requirements can limit their use to the richest companies. In other words, PETs have done more to entrench power than to undermine it. Our work is therefore to propose a newer framework for PET evaluation that takes these aspects into account instead of just focusing mathematical amusements that enable privacy-preserving surveillance.

Computer science isn't any more neutral than other sciences and we should expect practioners to behave accordingly. I look forward to finishing the paper with the collaboration.
